readerTitle: Three ways to earn 10% more. Only one doubles profit.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (회계 대행사, 비스트로) + 실제 연구 (Marn & Rosiello, 1992). 기업 사례보다 계산으로 보여주는 편이 개념에 맞아 numbers_twist로 바꿈
insight: 가격, 판매량, 비용은 같은 비율로 움직여도 이익에 주는 효과가 다르다. 그 순위는 사업의 비용 구조가 정한다.
misconception: 이익을 늘리려면 고객을 더 모으는 것이 가장 확실하다. 10% 개선이면 어느 쪽이든 효과가 비슷하다.

sources.text: Marn, M. V., & Rosiello, R. L. (1992). Managing Price, Gaining Profit. Harvard Business Review.
회계 대행사와 비스트로 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Marn & Rosiello(1992) 수치 확인 필요: 대형 기업 평균 기준 가격 1% 개선 시 영업이익 약 11.1%, 변동비 1% 절감 약 7.8%, 판매량 1% 증가 약 3.3%, 고정비 1% 절감 약 2.3%로 기억함. 표본 수(약 2,400개 기업, Compustat)도 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 'thousands of large companies', 'about 11% / 8% / 3%'로만 적었습니다.
가격 인상 후 고객 이탈 한도: 공헌이익 $350 × N − $25,000 ≥ $5,000 → N ≥ 85.7. 86명이면 $5,100, 85명이면 $4,750이므로 최대 14명 이탈까지 이익 유지.

cards.title: Three ways to earn 10% more. Only one doubles profit.
body: A small bookkeeping firm makes $5,000 a month in profit. The owner has three ideas, and each one is a 10% change.
On paper they sound equal. On the profit line, they are not even close.

image.label: Three levers on a machine, one pulled further than the others
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 기계에 레버 세 개, 라벨은 "Price", "Volume", "Cost". 각 레버 위 계기판 바늘이 서로 다르게 움직이고 "Price" 쪽 바늘이 가장 크게 올라감. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Which 10% move adds the most profit?
body: Your bookkeeping firm has 100 clients paying $500 a month. Each client costs $200 a month in software and contractor hours. Salaries and rent cost $25,000 a month.
Profit: $5,000 a month. You can push one lever by 10%.

options.feedback: It adds only $3,000. Each new client brings $200 of its own costs, so just $300 of every $500 reaches profit.

options.text: Raise prices 10% and keep every client
options.feedback: It adds $5,000, so profit doubles. A price rise brings no new costs with it. The hard part is keeping the clients.
It adds $4,500, a close second. But most of those costs are salaries, and a 10% cut often means fewer people or slower service.

cards.title: Same 10%, very different results.
body: Starting profit was $5,000. The price rise doubled it. Winning more clients, the move most owners try first, added the least.

image.label: Same 10%, very different results.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: The three profit levers
body: Profit has only three levers: **price**, **volume** (how much you sell) and **cost**. Every plan to earn more pulls at least one of them.
*Profit = (price − cost per sale) × volume − fixed costs.*
The levers are not equal. Extra price arrives with no new costs. Extra volume brings its own costs along. That is why the same 10% moves profit by such different amounts.

image.label: Profit formula with three levers labeled
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 공식 "(Price − Cost per sale) × Volume − Fixed costs = Profit"을 크게 쓰고, Price, Volume, Cost 아래에 각각 작은 레버 아이콘. Price에서 Profit으로 곧장 이어지는 굵은 화살표, Volume에서는 중간에 비용이 빠져나가는 얇은 화살표.

cards.title: Large companies show the same pattern.
body: In a 1992 Harvard Business Review article, McKinsey consultants Michael Marn and Robert Rosiello looked at average results across thousands of large companies.
A 1% price rise, with sales volume unchanged, lifted operating profit by about 11%. A 1% cut in the costs tied to each sale lifted it by about 8%. A 1% rise in volume lifted it by only about 3%.
Exact numbers differ by business. The order is what surprised managers.

cards.title: Your cost structure sets the ranking.
body: When each sale carries heavy costs, like a grocer paying for the goods on its shelves, the cost lever is strong and volume is weak. Little of each extra sale is left over.
When each sale carries almost no cost, volume gets close to price in power. So rank your own levers before copying someone else's playbook.
cards.softwareNote: A software product that keeps about $90 of every extra $100 in sales gains almost as much from a new customer as from a price rise. That is one reason software firms often chase growth so hard.

cards.title: The levers pull on each other.
body: Raise prices and some customers may leave. Cut costs and quality can slip, which hurts volume later. No lever moves alone.

So ask a sharper question: how much of one lever can I lose and still come out ahead? In the bookkeeping firm, the 10% price rise still earns at least as much **even if up to 14 of 100 clients leave**. That gives the owner a clear test before acting.

cards.title: Now it's a bistro.
body: Your bistro serves 5,000 meals a month at a $20 average. Food and supplies cost $7 a meal. Rent and staff cost $60,000 a month. Profit: $5,000.
You have time for one project this month. Which do you pick?

image.label: Bistro owner comparing three notes on a counter
image.brief: 작은 비스트로 카운터에 메모 세 장: "Prices +5%", "Promo: 5% more meals", "Cheaper ingredients". 주인이 계산기를 들고 고민하는 장면. 따뜻한 조명, 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

options.text: Raise prices 5% and track meal counts every week
options.feedback: It adds up to $5,000. You could lose about 350 meals a month, around 7%, and still earn what you earn today, so weekly counts tell you if it's working.

options.text: Run a promotion to serve 5% more meals
options.feedback: 250 more meals leave $13 each, or $3,250, before the promotion's own cost. Any discount shrinks that further.

options.text: Switch to cheaper ingredients to cut food costs 5%
options.feedback: It saves only $1,750 a month. If regulars taste the difference, every lost meal costs you $13.

cards.title: Price, volume, cost: test all three before you pull one.
body: The same percentage change can double profit or barely move it. Work out what each lever adds, then ask how much you could lose on another and still win.
**Try it today:** take last month's numbers. Calculate what 5% on price, on volume and on costs would each add to profit.
